Q01.sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  customer_id,
  total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
  AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
  AND status = 'DELIVERED'
ORDER BY order_id
Q01.rationale: Avoids the costly STRFTIME call on every row by using a lexical range on the ISO‑8601 stored date. The predicate is sargable and can exploit an index on order_date if one is added later, while remaining semantically identical for all possible rows.

Q01.sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  customer_id,
  total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE substr(order_date, 1, 4) = '2024'
  AND status = 'DELIVERED'
ORDER BY order_id
Q01.rationale: Extracts the year with a simple substring instead of STRFTIME, which is cheaper because it avoids a function call and a cast. The result set is unchanged because order_date is stored as 'YYYY‑MM‑DD'.

Q01.sql:
WITH orders_2024 AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount, status
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount
FROM orders_2024
WHERE status = 'DELIVERED'
ORDER BY order_id
Q01.rationale: Materialises the subset of 2024 orders once in a CTE, then applies the status filter and final projection. This can help the optimizer reuse the filtered rows and reduces repeated evaluation of the date expression, while producing exactly the same rows and order.

Q01.sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  customer_id,
  total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE
  (
    order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
  )
  AND status = 'DELIVERED'
ORDER BY
  order_id NULLS LAST
Q01.rationale: Rewrites functions/arithmetic applied to columns (EXTRACT(YEAR ...), col / k) into range predicates on the bare column so indexes and partition pruning can be used.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  name,
  unit_price
FROM products
WHERE category_id IN (9, 13, 17, 21)
  AND unit_price > 40
ORDER BY product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.rationale: Replacing the OR chain with a single IN predicate lets SQLite treat the condition as a set membership test, which is evaluated more compactly during the table scan. The semantics are identical because IN on a list of constants is equivalent to the series of ORs, and the additional unit_price filter is unchanged.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  p.unit_price
FROM products AS p
JOIN (VALUES (9), (13), (17), (21)) AS v(cat_id) ON p.category_id = v.cat_id
WHERE p.unit_price > 40
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.rationale: Creating a tiny derived table of the wanted category ids and joining it eliminates the repeated column comparisons. SQLite can perform a fast hash‑join between the 4‑row VALUES table and the products scan, yielding the same rows but with fewer predicate evaluations per product.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  p.unit_price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.unit_price > 40
  AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES (9), (13), (17), (21)) AS v(cat_id)
    WHERE v.cat_id = p.category_id
  )
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.rationale: An EXISTS test against the same VALUES list is logically equivalent to the IN predicate but forces SQLite to use a correlated semi‑join, which can be more efficient on very small lookup sets because the engine can stop scanning the VALUES table after the first match. The result set and ordering remain unchanged.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  name,
  unit_price
FROM products
WHERE
  (
    category_id IN (9, 13, 17, 21)
  ) AND unit_price > 40
ORDER BY
  product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.rationale: Collapses an OR chain of equalities on one column into an IN list.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  products.product_id AS product_id,
  products.name AS name,
  products.unit_price AS unit_price
FROM products AS products
WHERE
  (
    products.category_id = 13
    OR products.category_id = 17
    OR products.category_id = 21
    OR products.category_id = 9
  )
  AND products.unit_price > 40
ORDER BY
  product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.rationale: Pushes predicates down into derived tables and join conditions (sqlglot pushdown_predicates).

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  p.unit_price
FROM products AS p
JOIN (
    SELECT 9  AS cat_id UNION ALL
    SELECT 13 UNION ALL
    SELECT 17 UNION ALL
    SELECT 21
) AS v ON p.category_id = v.cat_id
WHERE p.unit_price > 40
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.strategy: Semi‑join via derived UNION ALL table
Q02.rationale: SQLite does not support the VALUES clause as a table source with column aliases. Replacing it with a UNION ALL derived table provides the same set of category IDs, allowing the join to be performed as a semi‑join. The query remains semantically identical to the original, preserving NULL handling (category_id is NOT NULL) and ordering.

Q02.sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  p.unit_price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.unit_price > 40
  AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM (
            SELECT 9  AS cat_id UNION ALL
            SELECT 13 UNION ALL
            SELECT 17 UNION ALL
            SELECT 21
        ) AS v
        WHERE v.cat_id = p.category_id
    )
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q02.strategy: EXISTS anti‑correlated subquery with UNION ALL derived table
Q02.rationale: The original EXISTS version used a VALUES table, which SQLite rejects. Substituting a UNION ALL derived table yields an equivalent set of allowed category IDs. The EXISTS predicate correctly implements the same filter semantics as the original OR list, and the overall query returns the same rows in the same order.

Q03.sql:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE total_amount > 800
ORDER BY total_amount DESC,
         order_id ASC
LIMIT 50
Q03.rationale: The original condition `CAST(total_amount AS REAL) / 2 > 400` is equivalent to `total_amount > 800` because total_amount is already stored as REAL and never NULL. Pushing this simple predicate into the scan reduces the number of rows that must be sorted, eliminating the need for the temporary B‑tree used for ordering the full table.

Q03.sql:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE total_amount * 0.5 > 400
ORDER BY total_amount DESC,
         order_id ASC
LIMIT 50
Q03.rationale: Multiplying both sides avoids a division and a CAST, keeping the expression sargable. `total_amount * 0.5 > 400` is the same as `total_amount > 800`. This lets SQLite apply the filter earlier and sort fewer rows, improving I/O and CPU usage.

Q03.sql:
WITH filtered AS (
    SELECT order_id,
           order_date,
           total_amount
    FROM orders
    WHERE total_amount > 800
)
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       total_amount
FROM filtered
ORDER BY total_amount DESC,
         order_id ASC
LIMIT 50
Q03.rationale: A Common Table Expression isolates the inexpensive predicate, allowing the optimiser to treat the CTE as a materialised filtered set. The outer query only needs to sort this smaller set, avoiding the temp B‑tree on the full table while preserving exact semantics, column order and limits.

Q04.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name,
  c.segment
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.segment = 'CORPORATE'
  AND c.is_active = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q04.rationale: customer_id is the primary key, so each row is already unique. Dropping DISTINCT removes an unnecessary distinct‑sort phase while preserving the result set and ordering.

Q04.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name,
  c.segment
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.segment = 'CORPORATE'
  AND c.is_active = 1
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name, c.segment
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q04.rationale: A GROUP BY on the primary‑key column produces the same unique rows as DISTINCT but lets SQLite use a simple aggregation pass without a separate distinct‑elimination step, which can be cheaper on a table‑scan.

Q04.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name,
  c.segment
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM customers AS c2
        WHERE c2.customer_id = c.customer_id
          AND c2.segment = 'CORPORATE'
          AND c2.is_active = 1
      )
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q04.rationale: Materialise the qualifying keys in a lightweight sub‑query and filter the main table with EXISTS. This decorrelates the predicate, allowing SQLite to stop scanning once the primary‑key match is found for each row, and still yields exactly the same rows.

Q04.sql:

Q05.sql:
SELECT
  status,
  ship_mode,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(SUM(total_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED')
GROUP BY status, ship_mode
ORDER BY status, ship_mode
Q05.rationale: The HAVING clause only tests the non‑aggregated columns status and ship_mode, so it can be moved to a WHERE predicate. This reduces the number of rows that must be grouped and eliminates the temporary B‑Tree used for the HAVING filter.

Q05.sql:
WITH filtered AS (
  SELECT status, ship_mode, total_amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE status IN ('SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED')
)
SELECT
  status,
  ship_mode,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(SUM(total_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM filtered
GROUP BY status, ship_mode
ORDER BY status, ship_mode
Q05.rationale: A CTE isolates the small filtered set before aggregation. SQLite can materialise the CTE once and then perform a single‑pass GROUP BY on the already‑filtered rows, avoiding a second scan of the full orders table.

Q05.sql:
SELECT
  status,
  ship_mode,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(SUM(total_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED')
GROUP BY status, ship_mode
ORDER BY status, ship_mode
Q05.rationale: Both status and ship_mode are defined as NOT NULL, so the explicit "NULLS LAST" clause is unnecessary. Removing it lets SQLite recognise that the GROUP BY order already satisfies the ORDER BY, avoiding the temporary B‑Tree for sorting.

Q05.sql:
SELECT
  status,

Q06.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name
FROM   customers AS c
WHERE  EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
         FROM   orders AS o
         WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
           AND  o.order_date >= '2025-06-01'
           AND  o.total_amount > 500
       )
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q06.rationale: Replaces the IN subquery with a correlated EXISTS predicate, allowing SQLite to use a semi‑join instead of materialising a temporary table. The predicate is sargable on orders.order_date and orders.total_amount, so the engine can stop scanning orders as soon as a matching row is found for each customer.

Q06.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id,
                c.name
FROM   customers AS c
JOIN   orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.order_date >= '2025-06-01'
      AND o.total_amount > 500
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q06.rationale: Joins customers directly to qualifying orders and uses DISTINCT to remove duplicates. SQLite can perform the join in a single pass over orders (filtered by the date and amount predicates) and then project the distinct customer rows, avoiding the subquery overhead.

Q06.sql:
WITH qualified_customers AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
    FROM   orders AS o
    WHERE  o.order_date >= '2025-06-01'
      AND  o.total_amount > 500
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name
FROM   customers AS c
JOIN   qualified_customers qc ON qc.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q06.rationale: Materialises the filtered set of qualifying customers once in a CTE, then simply joins to it. The CTE can be evaluated once, and the outer query just scans the primary‑key index of customers, which is the fastest access path for the final projection.

  c.name AS name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN (

Q07.sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name
FROM products AS p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_items AS oi
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
)
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q07.rationale: Rewrites the IN‑subquery as a correlated NOT EXISTS, allowing SQLite to use a semi‑join anti‑join implementation that can stop scanning order_items as soon as a match is found, reducing work compared to scanning the entire subquery result set.

Q07.sql:

  p.name
FROM products AS p
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.product_id NULLS LAST
Q07.rationale: Transforms the anti‑join into a LEFT OUTER JOIN followed by an IS NULL filter; SQLite can treat this as an anti‑join and avoid materialising the subquery, using the primary‑key index on order_items(product_id) for fast look‑ups.

Q07.sql:

  p.name
FROM products AS p
EXCEPT

  oi.product_id,
  '' AS name
FROM order_items AS oi
ORDER BY product_id NULLS LAST
Q07.rationale: Uses set‑difference (EXCEPT) which SQLite executes as a distinct‑preserving operation; because product_id is unique, the result is identical and SQLite can implement the difference with a merge‑join style algorithm that is often faster than evaluating an IN list.

JOIN order_items AS oi ON p2.product_id = oi.product_id
ORDER BY product_id NULLS LAST

The second query must return the same columns (product_id, name) for those products, so we join back to products to retrieve the name. This preserves the original semantics, including NULL handling and ordering, while allowing the optimizer to treat the operation as a set difference.

Q08.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.name
FROM products AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM order_items AS oi
        JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
          AND o.status = 'RETURNED'
      )
ORDER BY p.product_id
Q08.rationale: Replace the three‑way join plus DISTINCT with a semi‑join expressed via EXISTS. The subquery stops as soon as it finds a matching returned order, so each product is visited only once and no temporary B‑tree for DISTINCT or ORDER BY is required.

Q08.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.name
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.product_id IN (
        SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
        FROM order_items AS oi
        JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE o.status = 'RETURNED'
      )
ORDER BY p.product_id
Q08.rationale: Use a single IN clause that selects distinct product_id values from order_items of returned orders. SQLite can materialize the subquery once and use the primary‑key lookup for products, avoiding the row‑by‑row join and the temporary DISTINCT on the outer query.

Q08.sql:

       p.name
FROM (
        SELECT oi.product_id
        FROM order_items AS oi
        JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE o.status = 'RETURNED'
        GROUP BY oi.product_id
      ) AS q
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = q.product_id
ORDER BY p.product_id
Q08.rationale: Aggregate in the inner query to deduplicate product_id before joining to products. GROUP BY is cheaper than DISTINCT on a large join because it can be satisfied with a hash‑aggregate, and the outer join then returns each product exactly once without a separate DISTINCT step.

Q09.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name,
  COALESCE(o_agg.order_count, 0) AS order_count,
  o_agg.last_order
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT
    o.customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order
  FROM orders AS o
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
) AS o_agg ON o_agg.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.nation_id = 7
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q09.rationale: Aggregates orders per customer in a single scan and left‑joins the result to the filtered customers, eliminating two correlated subqueries and allowing SQLite to use the automatic covering index on orders.customer_id once.

Q09.sql:
WITH filtered_customers AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name
  FROM customers
  WHERE nation_id = 7
),
order_stats AS (
  SELECT
    o.customer_id,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id) AS order_count,
    MAX(o.order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id) AS last_order
  FROM orders AS o
  WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM filtered_customers fc WHERE fc.customer_id = o.customer_id)
)
SELECT
  fc.customer_id,
  fc.name,
  COALESCE(os.order_count, 0) AS order_count,
  os.last_order
FROM filtered_customers AS fc
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, order_count, last_order
  FROM order_stats
) AS os ON os.customer_id = fc.customer_id
ORDER BY fc.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q09.rationale: Computes order count and last order date with window functions over the orders of the required nation, then selects distinct customer rows. This avoids per‑row subquery execution and lets SQLite materialise the window once.

Q09.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name,
  COALESCE(a.order_count, 0) AS order_count,
  a.last_order
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT
    o.customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order
  FROM orders AS o
  WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM customers AS c2
    WHERE c2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND c2.nation_id = 7
  )
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
) AS a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.nation_id = 7
ORDER BY c.customer_id NULLS LAST
Q09.rationale: Uses an EXISTS predicate to restrict orders to the relevant customers, then aggregates in a single derived table. This keeps the semantics identical (NULL when no orders) while allowing SQLite to apply the covering index only once.

SELECT

  (
